19 A car of mass 1400 kg is travelling on a straight, horizontal road at a constant speed of 25 m s–1.
The output power from the car’s engine is 30 kW.
The car then travels up a slope at 2° to the horizontal, maintaining the same constant speed.
1400 kg
25 m s–1
25 m s–1
2°
What is the output power of the car’s engine when travelling up the slope?
A
12 kW
B
31 kW
C
42 kW
D
65 kW

hints: Notice the speed stays at $25\text{ m s}^{-1}$ on both the flat and the $2^{\circ}$ slope, so resultant force is zero and engine force balances resistive force plus any weight component.
Recall $P = Fv$ for motion with force parallel to velocity, so first find the resistive force on the flat from $F = P/v$ using $30\text{ kW}$ and $25\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
On the slope add the component of weight down the slope, $mg\sin2^{\circ}$, to that resistive force, then multiply the total forward force by $25\text{ m s}^{-1}$ to get the new power.
walkthrough: Constant speed means zero acceleration, so driving force equals opposing force. On the horizontal road the only opposition is air resistance and friction.
Use $P = Fv$ rearranged to $F = P/v$. With $P = 30000\text{ W}$ and $v = 25\text{ m s}^{-1}$, $F = 30000/25 = 1200\text{ N}$. This resistive force is assumed the same on the slope.
Up the $2^{\circ}$ slope the engine must also balance the component of weight down the slope, $mg\sin\theta$. With $m = 1400\text{ kg}$, this is $1400 \times 9.81 \times \sin2^{\circ}$.
Calculate the extra force: $\sin2^{\circ} \approx 0.0349$, so $F_{hill} \approx 1400 \times 9.81 \times 0.0349 \approx 479\text{ N}$.
Total driving force uphill is $1200 + 479 \approx 1679\text{ N}$. New power is $P = Fv = 1679 \times 25 \approx 42000\text{ W} \approx 42\text{ kW}$.
Equivalently, extra power is $mgv\sin\theta \approx 12\text{ kW}$ added to $30\text{ kW}$. This is option C.

A.explanation: Too small because the slope requires extra power against gravity, so power cannot fall from $30\text{ kW}$ to $12\text{ kW}$ at the same $25\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

B.explanation: Only $1\text{ kW}$ more than on the flat, which greatly underestimates the extra $mg\sin2^{\circ}v$ power needed to gain gravitational potential energy.

C.explanation: Adds the hill power $mg\sin2^{\circ}v \approx 12\text{ kW}$ to the $30\text{ kW}$ needed for resistive forces, giving about $42\text{ kW}$.

D.explanation: Too large because it adds much more than the true downslope weight component $mg\sin2^{\circ} \approx 480\text{ N}$ times $25\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
